text: How would you find two numbers in an array that add up to a target value? Talk me through your approach and its complexity.
answer: I would start with brute force: try every pair using two nested loops, which is Big O of n squared time and constant space. It is simple, but it does not scale, and the wasted work is searching for each number's partner. So I would use a hash map in one pass. For each number, I compute the complement, which is the target minus that number, and check whether the complement is already in the map. If it is, I return the pair. If not, I store the current number with its index and continue. That gives Big O of n average time and Big O of n space. Checking before inserting matters for duplicates, because it stops an element from pairing with itself, while two real threes still work for a target of six. If no pair exists, the loop finishes and I return an empty result or null, depending on what we agree. I would also confirm whether multiple answers are possible.

text: How would you check whether a string of brackets is balanced?
expected: empty string and unmatched closing bracket
answer: A stack is the natural choice, because the most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed. I walk through the string one character at a time. When I see an opening bracket, I push it onto the stack. When I see a closing bracket, I look at the top of the stack and check that it is the matching type, using a small map from each closing bracket to its opening partner. So a closing parenthesis must match an opening parenthesis, and a closing square bracket must match an opening square bracket. If they do not match, I return false. If I hit a closing bracket while the stack is empty, that bracket is unmatched, so I also return false right away. At the end, the string is balanced only if the stack is empty, which catches leftover opening brackets. An empty string counts as balanced. This takes Big O of n time and, in the worst case, Big O of n space.

text: How would you reverse a singly linked list? Explain iterative and recursive options.
answer: For the iterative version, I keep three pointers: previous, which starts as null, current, which starts at the head, and next. On each step I save current's next node so I do not lose the rest of the list, point current's next backward at previous, then move previous and current forward by one. When current becomes null, previous is the new head. That is Big O of n time and Big O of one space. For the recursive version, I reverse everything after the head, which returns the new head, then make the node after the head point back to the head and set the head's next to null. The code is neat and still Big O of n time, but it uses Big O of n stack space, so a very long list could overflow the stack. Both handle the edge cases naturally: for an empty list or a single node, I just return the head unchanged, which is also the recursive base case.

text: How would you find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters?
answer: A sliding window fits well here. Two pointers, left and right, mark a window that never contains a repeated character, and I extend the right pointer one character at a time. Alongside that, I keep a hash map from each character to the last index where I saw it. When the right pointer reaches a character already in the map, I may need to move the left edge to one past that previous position. The important detail is that left must never move backward, so I take the maximum of the current left and last seen index plus one. Without that, a repeat from before the window, as in a string like a b b a, would wrongly shrink my progress and produce an invalid window. After each step, I update the character's position and the best length, which is right minus left plus one. Each character is processed once, giving Big O of n time, with space bounded by the character set size.

text: How would you merge a list of overlapping intervals?
answer: Sorting the intervals comes first, so I would order them by start value, because once they are ordered, any interval that overlaps the current merged one must come right after it. Then I scan through them, keeping a result list. For each interval, if its start is less than or equal to the end of the last interval in the result, they overlap, so I set that last end to the maximum of the two ends. The maximum matters because one interval can sit completely inside another, like one to ten and two to three. Otherwise, there is no overlap, so I append it as a new interval. Touching intervals, like one to three and three to five, are worth clarifying. With closed ranges I would merge them, which is what less than or equal does, but with half-open ranges or a strict rule I would use strictly less than. Sorting dominates, giving Big O of n log n time, and the output takes Big O of n space.

text: How would you design an LRU cache with constant-time get and put?
expected: hash map plus doubly linked list
answer: The classic design combines a hash map with a doubly linked list. The map goes from key to list node, so finding an item is constant time, and the list keeps items in usage order, with the most recently used at the head and the least recently used at the tail. Dummy head and tail nodes keep the pointer logic clean. On get, I look up the node, and if it exists I unlink it, move it to the front, and return its value. On put with an existing key, I update the value and move it to the front the same way. For a new key at capacity, I evict the tail's node and delete its key from the map, then insert the new node at the front. Every step is pointer updates plus hash lookups, so both operations are Big O of one on average. For thread safety, even get changes the list, so a simple mutex works, and sharding the cache into segments reduces contention.

text: How would you find the k most frequent words in a large text?
expected: heap of size k or bucket sort
ties and memory for very large input
answer: This breaks into counting, then selecting. I count every word with a hash map, which is linear in the total number of words, after normalizing case. To select the top k, I could keep a min-heap of size k: push each unique word, and when the heap exceeds k, pop the smallest. With m unique words, that is Big O of m log k time and Big O of k extra space, which is great when k is small. Alternatively, bucket sort uses frequency as an index, since no count can exceed the total word count, giving linear time but more memory. A full sort would be Big O of m log m. For ties, I would ask for a rule, such as alphabetical order, and build it into the comparison. If the input does not fit in memory, I would hash words into partitions on disk, count each partition, and merge the results, or use a distributed job, or a count-min sketch if approximate answers are acceptable.

text: How would you detect a cycle in a linked list?
expected: finding the cycle start as an extension
answer: The simplest approach is a hash set. I walk the list and store each node's reference, not its value, since values can repeat. If I reach a node already in the set, there is a cycle, and if I reach null, there is not. That is Big O of n time, but also Big O of n space. To bring space down to Big O of one, I would use fast and slow pointers, also known as Floyd's algorithm. Slow moves one step at a time and fast moves two. If there is no cycle, fast reaches the end. If there is one, fast eventually catches slow inside the loop, still in Big O of n time. As an extension, to find where the cycle starts, I leave one pointer at the meeting point and move the other back to the head. Then I advance both one step at a time, and the node where they meet is the start of the cycle.

text: Given a grid of land and water, how would you count the number of islands?
answer: Think of the grid as a graph, where each land cell connects to its neighboring land cells, so counting islands means counting connected components. I loop over every cell, and when I find land that has not been visited, I add one to my count and run a depth-first or breadth-first search from it to reach the whole island. As I visit cells, I mark them, either by overwriting them with water or using a separate visited grid if I should not change the input. That marking stops me from counting the same island twice or looping forever. Before coding, I would ask whether diagonal neighbors count, since that changes four directions into eight and can change the answer. Each cell is processed a constant number of times, so time is Big O of rows times columns. Space is the same in the worst case. On very large grids, recursive depth-first search can overflow the stack, so I would prefer breadth-first search or an explicit stack.

text: How would you find the shortest path between two nodes in an unweighted graph? What changes if edges have weights?
expected: tracking parents to rebuild the path
answer: For an unweighted graph, I would use breadth-first search, because it explores nodes in order of distance, so the first time I reach the target, I have found a path with the fewest edges. I use a queue and a visited set, and I mark nodes when enqueuing them. To return the actual path, I record each node's parent when I discover it, then walk back from the target and reverse the result. That takes Big O of V plus E time and Big O of V space. If edges have non-negative weights, the fewest edges may no longer be the cheapest route, so I would switch to Dijkstra's algorithm. It uses a priority queue, always settles the unvisited node with the lowest known distance, relaxes its edges, and tracks parents the same way. With a binary heap, that is Big O of E log V time. If negative weights are possible, Dijkstra is not valid, so I would use Bellman-Ford instead, which is Big O of V times E.

text: How would you implement a function that debounces another function?
answer: Debouncing means the wrapped function only runs after calls have stopped for a set delay, which is useful for something like a search box. I would write a higher-order function that takes the function and the delay, and returns a new function. That returned function forms a closure over a timer variable, so the timer persists between calls and each debounced function has its own. On every call, I clear any existing timer and start a new one, so each call resets the wait, and the target only fires once the calls go quiet. To preserve context, I capture the arguments with rest parameters and the value of this, then invoke the original with apply when the timer fires. Finally, the default is trailing edge, firing after the pause. A leading edge option fires immediately on the first call, then ignores calls until the delay passes. I might also add a cancel method.

text: How would you determine whether a binary tree is a valid binary search tree?
expected: min and max bounds per node
common mistake of checking only children
answer: The cleanest check validates each node against a range, using a recursive function that takes a node plus a minimum and maximum bound, starting with no limits at the root. Each value must fall strictly inside its range. Going left, the node's value becomes the new maximum, and going right, it becomes the new minimum. This avoids the common mistake of checking only that a left child is smaller and a right child is larger than its parent. That misses violations deeper down. For example, a root of ten can have a right child of fifteen whose left child is six. Each local check passes, but six sits in the root's right subtree, so the tree is invalid. An alternative is an in-order traversal, because a valid search tree visits values in strictly increasing order, so I just compare each value to the previous one. Both are Big O of n time, with Big O of h space for tree height h. I would confirm how duplicates are treated.

text: Given a number of stairs, in how many ways can you climb them taking one or two steps at a time? Explain your reasoning.
answer: The trick is to think about the very last step. To reach stair n, I must have come from stair n minus one with a single step, or from stair n minus two with a double step. So the number of ways to reach n is the ways to reach n minus one plus the ways to reach n minus two, which is the Fibonacci recurrence. The base cases are one way for zero stairs, meaning do nothing, and one way for one stair, which gives two ways for two stairs. Plain recursion recomputes the same values and takes exponential time. Memoization fixes that by storing each result, giving Big O of n time and space. Better still, I can work upward iteratively. Since each value only depends on the previous two, I keep two variables and update them as I go, for Big O of n time and Big O of one space. For large n, I would also watch for integer overflow.

text: How would you find the median of a stream of numbers as they arrive?
answer: Two heaps solve this neatly by splitting the numbers in half. A max-heap holds the lower half, so its top is the largest of the small numbers, and a min-heap holds the upper half, so its top is the smallest of the large numbers. The median is always at those tops. When a number arrives, I compare it with the top of the max-heap and push it to the correct side. Then I rebalance: if the two sizes differ by more than one, I move a top element across. For an odd count, the median is the top of the heap with one extra element. For an even count, it is the average of both tops. Insert is Big O of log n and reading the median is Big O of one, with Big O of n space because every number is stored. If the stream is unbounded, I would consider a sliding window, counting buckets for a limited value range, or an approximate quantile sketch such as t-digest.
